name: Ivan Zhang

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: I’m a senior researcher with the Work Futures Panel, an independent group. We have no ties to AI companies, employers, unions, political parties or government; we sell nothing and campaign for no side. Your answers are confidential. What does your usual shift involve?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I’m 58 and lead an afternoon team answering parcel-delivery calls and chats. My two-year college diploma is in logistics, and I am usually the one who untangles a package that has three scans but no recipient. I use the approved AI case summary now and then, after another agent has tested it; the depot scan and driver note still decide what we tell a customer. My pay is ordinary for a contact-centre lead, even though colleagues bring me the hardest complaints.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: What is behind the decisions you make about this job?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: My wife Mei works at a small alterations shop, and our grown children live separately. We rent, have about four months of expenses saved, and there are some other centres within a workable bus ride. Mei’s hours vary with orders, so I count what she actually earns rather than a promised week. We have not confirmed what income we would have if I stopped paid work.

I would show colleagues the **false delivery scan** I checked against depot history.
think: I think our **afternoon team** keeps its work if AI saves only small amounts of time.
I know Mei’s **variable shop hours** make the four-month reserve worth checking.
do: Keep **paid parcel calls** and verify depot scans against approved AI summaries.
Compare **actual wages**, rent and existing savings each month without treating the check as new saving.
feel: I feel **calm** about steady work, while keeping an eye on household costs.

fieldNote: He uses **AI occasionally** after others test it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would say a quicker case summary is useful if it points to the right tracking number. Yesterday a parcel showed “delivered” at the depot before the driver had loaded it, so I checked the second scan. I would not let a short note outrank the scan history.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately I think our afternoon team keeps its work in this version. Four months saved gives Mei and me some breathing room, though her shop hours vary. I want to hold on to the skill that people ask for when the screen and the driver disagree.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would keep the paid afternoon rota and check depot scans against the approved summaries as I do now. At the end of each month I would put the real rent and Mei’s actual wages beside my payslip, so we know whether four months still means four months. I would not change jobs because a summary saves a minute.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I feel calm about this picture. Parcel mistakes still need someone to follow the trail. The household budget deserves a check even when work is steady.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you call the driver after hours to settle a disputed delivery?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The driver note can arrive late, so I call the depot on a paid shift if the scans disagree. I would not message the driver privately after work. A customer should hear what we have verified, not what the summary guesses.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Does that monthly budget check mean you are saving more?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: No, the monthly sheet does not mean we are putting more money aside yet. It just tells us what the existing four-month reserve would cover at current costs. If the rent changes, the number changes.

Compare actual wages, rent and existing savings each month

fieldNote: He will test the **new sorter** only with approval, de-identified closed cases and paid time.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would tell the team that easy “where is my parcel” chats could move to AI, while damaged and missing parcels land on fewer agents. I would ask the manager for the written afternoon rota and a paid test of the new exception sorter. A demonstration is fine, but it does not show what happens when the driver scan is wrong.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I think some of my own paid hours could disappear if the queue shrinks. My logistics diploma and the difficult cases help, but no one has promised a full lead rota. Four months saved lets us compare options; it is not a substitute for a monthly wage.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: If the centre approves it and pays the time, I would learn the new AI exception sorter on fifteen closed missing-parcel cases, checking each result against depot scans. I would keep handling live disputes on my paid rota and ask for written weekly hours. If my afternoon hours are cut, I would compare posted paid depot-desk jobs by written weekly wages and hours covering rent, utilities and bus fare before applying.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I feel anxious about my own rota becoming shorter. I can learn a tested tool and there are some other centres, but a whole shift can vanish faster than four months of rent. I need numbers, not reassurance.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you test the sorter on current customers?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would use only closed cases cleared for testing, with customer names removed, and only during paid time. If the centre has not approved that test, I would wait rather than feed live claims into a new tool. The depot scans remain the check.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would a new depot desk have to pay?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would not leave for a better hourly rate attached to fewer days. I need a posted paid opening and a written full week that covers rent and utilities after the fare. I would stay on paid calls until a suitable offer is signed.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would tell Mei full AGI by 2028 could settle most tracking chats before the team can change its shifts. Robots lifting parcels around 2031 would arrive later; our screen work is the immediate target. I would ask the centre for actual paid shift dates, not assume it will keep a lead seat.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I think the afternoon rota could end, and four months saved would then start running down. Mei’s tailoring wage is useful but varies; it does not cover our rent and utilities alone. There are some centres nearby, but I do not know which will still have a paid desk.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: In 2026 I would put the last six full-week payslips beside rent, utilities and the bus fare. If paid afternoon calls end after 2028, I would apply for posted paid depot or service desks only where written weekly wages and hours cover those costs after travel, and the final bus fits the shift. I would keep my current paid calls until a suitable offer is signed; if no suitable opening follows the end, Mei and I would ask the landlord about dates for a possible payment plan before rent is late, without counting on agreement.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I feel anxious, close to alarmed when I picture the last paid shift. Four months gives me time for a search, but the same technology may reach the desks I would apply to. I can handle a lost parcel; I cannot guess a vacancy into being.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you begin using savings before a shift actually ends?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: No, I would not start spending the four months now. The six payslips and bills tell us how long the existing money would last if paid calls actually end. We would review the calculation with Mei before using it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Is the landlord plan already available to you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The landlord has not offered a plan. We would ask only if calls ended and there were no suitable paid opening, and we would take the real figures. I would not tell our children to cover the rent.

Apply after 2028 paid-call end: posted paid desk, written rent/utility-covering weekly wages/hours after fare, last bus

Ask landlord before rent late if paid calls end without suitable opening

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would tell the depot that five years is enough to show which scan errors the AI keeps missing. Thinking AGI could change our phones by 2031, while parcel robots might follow around 2034. I would rather have a paid desk that can correct a route record than a fancy title that only forwards a complaint.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I think a depot exception desk could use the fault trail I have learned over years, but I cannot assume one will open near us. My ordinary pay and four months saved give some room, not a licence to take an unpaid apprenticeship. Mei’s variable hours make the full week matter.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Starting in 2026 I would ask the depot supervisor whether a posted paid exception-desk role exists and what authority it has to correct scan records. If a paid opening is posted, I would apply only if written weekly wages and hours cover rent, utilities and bus fare, with the bus running at shift end. I would keep my paid calls until a suitable offer is signed; if no opening exists or my hours fall around 2031, I would check posted paid service-centre desks by the same figures.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I feel anxious about a shorter rota, though five years lets me make a proper comparison. I am not keen to jump at an unfamiliar desk on a verbal promise. An actual authority to fix a scan would make the move worth considering.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Is scan-correction authority a hard condition or something you want to understand?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I am asking about correction authority, not requiring a special badge. I would want to know whether the role can change a wrong delivery scan, because forwarding every case could be another shrinking queue. The written pay and hours are the conditions I cannot waive.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you wait until 2031 to search if no depot opening appears?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: If there is no depot opening, I would look at posted paid service-centre desks now, not wait until 2031. If my own hours later fall, I would widen the same search. I would still need a signed offer and a bus home before leaving.

transcript.text: AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would tell Mei a decade lets us check the household numbers each year instead of naming a stop-work date. Thinking AGI could change tracking work by 2036; robots at the depot would be later, around 2039. I would keep the afternoon desk while it pays and review the next step from actual figures.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I think I might still want paid work in ten years, but I cannot know what retirement income will be until we check it. Four months saved does not make a lifetime plan. I would like more evenings with Mei if her shop and my wage allow it, not because a scenario card names a year.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Each year I would compare our actual wages, rent, utilities, travel costs and any confirmed retirement income, using four months saved only as the present reserve. I would keep paid parcel calls while the hours remain. If hours fall after 2036 and we still need my wage, I would compare posted paid depot and service desks by written weekly wages and hours covering rent and utilities after fare, leaving only for a suitable signed offer and a bus home.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I feel fairly calm about time to prepare, with some unease about what our future income actually is. The current paid rota and some nearby jobs give us choices. I do not want to promise Mei an evening together by spending rent money.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you set a retirement date now?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: No, I would not pick a retirement date from the card. We would have to know what income is documented and what the bills actually cost then. If the figures do not fit, I keep earning.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you move to any depot desk if the call hours fell?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: A depot desk is one option, not a promise. I would check the written complete week, fare and final bus, then leave only once a suitable offer is signed. I will not ask our grown children to make up a missing wage.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: AGI by 2028 worries me most because it could end the afternoon rota while our four months saved become a countdown. Mei’s actual shop hours and our rent would set the pace of a search, not a clever headline. Written shift dates and posted paid desks with full-week wages and hours would help us decide.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: A parcel can have three scans and still be in the wrong town. I would ask who can correct the record before I tell a customer the package is coming tomorrow.
